Embryonic

/em-bree-ON-ik/ - the stress falls on ON · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Embryonic means in an early and undeveloped stage.

The peace talks remain embryonic — after a month, the two delegations have agreed only on the shape of the table.

Worked Example

In 1990 the country's democracy was embryonic: one independent newspaper run from a basement, a parliament that met in a gymnasium, a constitution that was still nine handwritten pages in a law professor's satchel. Foreign observers counted institutions and found almost nothing — which was the point. Almost nothing is what the earliest stage of anything looks like.

Embryonic is the exact word because it names what is in an early and undeveloped stage — formed enough to exist, too unformed to work at full size. It leans on biology's picture of the embryo: the design present, the parts barely sketched. Call a thing embryonic and you promise growth while admitting how little there is to show today.

How Embryonic Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

budding

budding: growth has broken the surface; embryonic is earlier still

undeveloped

undeveloped: plain and matter-of-fact — not yet grown, with no image behind it

Antonyms

full-grown

full-grown: development complete

fully-formed

fully-formed: every part already in its final shape

How Strong Is It? — embryonic → budding → full-blown

budding vs. embryonic

budding vs. embryonic: Budding goes past embryonic — the shape has broken the surface and anyone can watch it grow.

full-blown vs. embryonic

full-blown vs. embryonic: Full-blown is far stronger than embryonic: an embryonic plan is still a faint early sketch, while a full-blown one has gone all the way to its complete, finished form.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of embryonic.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — embryon

Root — embryon: the unformed young (Greek embryon, 'swelling within')

Suffix — -ic

Suffix — -ic: relating to

Put it together

Put it together: Embryon (the unformed young) + -ic (relating to) = like an embryo. The Greek packs a picture into the root itself: en ('within') plus bryein ('to swell') — something swelling into being inside its shell. English uses the literal sense in biology and borrows the picture for anything at its barely-begun stage.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Embryonic came into English whole, from Greek embryon — en ('within') plus bryein ('to swell'). The swelling root bry- built nothing else in everyday English; apart from embryo itself, this word has no common relatives to recognize it by.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / figurative

Embryonic suits plans, movements, and ventures at the barely-formed stage, and it quietly promises growth to come. Its opposite number in this unit is precocious, which praises a person for developing ahead of schedule — embryonic describes the thing itself, still barely begun. For plain factual smallness with no growth implied, undeveloped is the flatter choice.
